items.prompt: What is a 'fast-forward,' as this unit defines it?
choices: When the local branch's current commit is a direct ancestor of the remote's commit, so incorporating remote's changes just means moving the local pointer forward
Any merge that completes without conflicts
A special git command for speeding up large repositories
The process of squashing multiple commits into one
items.explanation: Fast-forward is a specific structural condition — local's ancestor relationship to remote — not a general description of a smooth merge.
items.reference:
Fast-forward
local HEAD is an ancestor of remote HEAD
no new commit needed — just move the pointer

Why: This is a narrow structural condition, not a synonym for "went smoothly."

items.prompt: Does a fast-forward create a new commit?
choices: No — it just moves the local branch pointer forward to the remote's commit
Yes, it always creates a merge commit with two parents
Yes, but only if there are no conflicts
It depends on how many files changed
items.explanation: Since nothing local diverged, there's nothing to reconcile — the pointer just advances, with no new commit created at all.
items.reference:
Fast-forward
local HEAD is an ancestor of remote HEAD
no new commit needed — just move the pointer

Why: This is a narrow structural condition, not a synonym for "went smoothly."

items.prompt: What is a 'merge commit'?
choices: A new commit with two parents, created when local history has diverged from remote, recording that both histories are now combined
Any commit that changes more than one file
A commit created automatically every time you run `git commit`
A commit that deletes conflicting changes automatically
items.explanation: A merge commit specifically has two parents — one for each side of the divergence — and exists to record that reconciliation actually happened.
items.reference:
Merge commit
two parents: local's last commit, remote's last commit
created when a fast-forward isn't possible

Why: It's git's honest record that real divergence happened — not a sign something went wrong.

items.prompt: When does git create a merge commit instead of a fast-forward?
choices: When local history has diverged from remote — both sides have added commits since their last common point
Every single time git pull is run, without exception
Only when a merge conflict occurs
Only when merging between two different repositories
items.explanation: Divergence — both sides having new commits since the common ancestor — is the specific condition that makes a fast-forward impossible and a merge commit necessary.
items.reference:
Merge commit
two parents: local's last commit, remote's last commit
created when a fast-forward isn't possible

Why: It's git's honest record that real divergence happened — not a sign something went wrong.

items.prompt: What does 'rebase' do, as this unit defines it?
choices: Replays local commits one by one on top of the remote's latest commit, producing a straight-line history
Deletes local commits that conflict with remote
Creates a merge commit with three parents instead of two
Reverts all local changes back to the last common ancestor
items.explanation: Rebase re-applies local commits' content onto a new base, producing new commits rather than a merge commit — the result reads as if local work started from the new base.
items.reference:
Rebase
replays local commits onto the new base
produces new commits, new hashes
no merge commit, straight-line history

Why: Rebase changes how history looks, not what content ultimately gets combined.

items.prompt: After a rebase, do the replayed local commits keep their original hash?
choices: No — each replayed commit gets a new hash, even though its message and change content stay the same
Yes, rebase always preserves the exact original commit hashes
Only the first replayed commit keeps its original hash
Hashes are irrelevant to how rebase works
items.explanation: Rebase creates new commits with new parents and new hashes — the original commits aren't modified, but replayed copies with different identities replace them in the new history.
items.reference:
Rebase
replays local commits onto the new base
produces new commits, new hashes
no merge commit, straight-line history

Why: Rebase changes how history looks, not what content ultimately gets combined.

items.prompt: What is 'divergence,' as this unit defines it?
choices: The state where local and remote both have commits the other doesn't, counted from their last common ancestor
Any difference in file content between two branches
A merge conflict that hasn't been resolved yet
The number of commits behind the main branch
items.explanation: Divergence is specifically about both sides having independently added commits since the branches were last in sync — this is exactly what makes a fast-forward impossible.
items.reference:
Divergence
both sides have new commits since the common ancestor
makes fast-forward impossible

Why: Divergence is a structural fact about the commit graph, not about how big or risky either side's changes are.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what caused Tuesday's pull to diverge when Monday's didn't?
choices: Local had made a commit since the last sync, giving it its own new history alongside remote's new commit
The remote repository was configured differently on Tuesday
Tuesday's commit was larger in file size than Monday's
Git randomly decides when to create merge commits
items.explanation: A single local commit since the last sync was enough to create divergence — the size or content of that commit doesn't matter, only the fact that both sides now have independent history.
items.reference:
Divergence
both sides have new commits since the common ancestor
makes fast-forward impossible

Why: Divergence is a structural fact about the commit graph, not about how big or risky either side's changes are.

items.prompt: In L2's fast-forward-not-possible diagram, why does commit B having two children (D and C) prevent a fast-forward?
choices: Neither D nor C is an ancestor of the other, so there's no single line of history to simply extend
Having two children is a git error state that must be fixed before continuing
B itself becomes corrupted when it gets a second child
It doesn't actually prevent a fast-forward — the diagram shows a fast-forward is still possible
items.explanation: Once B has two independent children, the ancestor relationship a fast-forward depends on no longer holds in either direction — a real reconciliation is required.
items.reference:
Two children, no ancestor relationship
B has two children: D (local) and C (remote)
neither is an ancestor of the other

Why: A fast-forward requires a single line of history to extend — two independent children break that.

items.prompt: What does it mean that 'neither D nor C is an ancestor of the other' in the diverged case?
choices: Walking backward from D never reaches C, and walking backward from C never reaches D — they're genuinely separate branches of history
It means D and C have identical content
It means one of the two commits must be deleted
It means the repository is corrupted and needs to be re-cloned
items.explanation: Tracing parent pointers from either commit never leads to the other — this is exactly the structural signature of divergence, requiring a merge commit or a rebase to reconcile.
items.reference:
Two children, no ancestor relationship
B has two children: D (local) and C (remote)
neither is an ancestor of the other

Why: A fast-forward requires a single line of history to extend — two independent children break that.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, are original commit hashes preserved by merge?
choices: Yes — merge keeps all original commits and their hashes exactly as they were
No — merge rewrites every commit's hash
Only the first commit's hash is preserved
Merge doesn't use hashes at all
items.explanation: Merge never modifies existing commits — it only adds a new merge commit on top, leaving every original commit's hash untouched.
items.reference:
Merge vs. rebase
New commit?merge: yes (1) / rebase: no (new hashes instead)
Hashes preserved?merge: yes / rebase: no
Shapemerge: branching / rebase: straight line

Why: This is exactly why rebase carries a real risk merge doesn't — rewritten hashes break anyone else's copy of the old commits.

items.prompt: According to L2's comparison table, what does the resulting history shape look like after a rebase, compared to a merge?
choices: Rebase produces a straight line, as if local work started from the new base; merge shows the actual branching and reconciliation point
Both produce identical history shapes
Rebase produces more branches than merge
Merge always produces a straight line, and rebase always shows branching
items.explanation: Rebase specifically erases the visible branching point by replaying commits onto the new base — merge preserves it as an honest record of the divergence.
items.reference:
Merge vs. rebase
New commit?merge: yes (1) / rebase: no (new hashes instead)
Hashes preserved?merge: yes / rebase: no
Shapemerge: branching / rebase: straight line

Why: This is exactly why rebase carries a real risk merge doesn't — rewritten hashes break anyone else's copy of the old commits.

items.prompt: Why is rebasing commits that have already been pushed and pulled by someone else risky?
choices: It rewrites hashes, leaving anyone who already has the old commits with history that now diverges from the rewritten version
Rebase always deletes the other person's local changes automatically
It's not actually risky — rebase is always safe regardless of sharing status
It only affects the remote repository's file permissions
items.explanation: Once other people have pulled the original commits, rewriting them via rebase creates two incompatible versions of the same history, which reconciling requires its own separate, messier process.
items.reference:
Rebase's real risk
rewritten hashes ≠ original hashes
others with the old commits now diverge from the rewritten history

Why: This trade-off is why merge is the safer default for already-shared history, even though rebase produces a cleaner-looking log.

items.prompt: Why is merge described as the safer default for history that's already been pushed and pulled by other people?
choices: Merge never rewrites existing commits, so it can't create the kind of hash mismatch rebase can
Merge is always faster to run than rebase
Merge automatically notifies every collaborator before running
Merge is safer only when working entirely alone on a repository
items.explanation: Because merge only adds a new commit on top rather than rewriting anything, it structurally can't produce the divergent-history problem that rebasing already-shared commits can.
items.reference:
Rebase's real risk
rewritten hashes ≠ original hashes
others with the old commits now diverge from the rewritten history

Why: This trade-off is why merge is the safer default for already-shared history, even though rebase produces a cleaner-looking log.

items.prompt: According to L2's generalizable lesson, does the fast-forward condition only apply to `git pull`?
choices: No — the same ancestor relationship governs every merge git performs, whether triggered by pull, an explicit merge, or a PR merge on GitHub
Yes, fast-forward is a concept unique to the pull command
No, but it only applies to merges done through a GUI tool, not the command line
Yes, but only for repositories hosted on GitHub specifically
items.explanation: The ancestor-relationship condition is a property of the commit graph itself — it governs the outcome the same way regardless of which git command or tool triggers the merge.
items.reference:
One structural fact, many triggers
same ancestor check
pull, explicit merge, PR merge — all governed the same way

Why: The visible outcome (clean update, merge commit, or rebase) always traces back to this one structural fact about the graph.

items.prompt: What single structural fact determines whether a merge is a clean fast-forward, a merge commit, or requires a rebase to avoid one?
choices: Whether one side's current commit is a strict ancestor of the other's, or whether the two sides have genuinely diverged
Which programming language the repository's code is written in
How many total commits exist in the repository's entire history
Whether the repository is public or private
items.explanation: The ancestor relationship between local and remote's current commits is the one fact that determines the outcome — everything else (fast-forward, merge commit, rebase) follows from it.
items.reference:
One structural fact, many triggers
same ancestor check
pull, explicit merge, PR merge — all governed the same way

Why: The visible outcome (clean update, merge commit, or rebase) always traces back to this one structural fact about the graph.

items.prompt: Implement `isAncestor(commits, ancestorId, descendantId)`, matching this unit's L3: walk backward from `descendantId` through parent pointers, returning `true` if `ancestorId` is found along the way, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: B is an ancestor of C
tests.expr: expect(isAncestor({ A: { id: 'A', parent: null }, B: { id: 'B', parent: 'A' }, C: { id: 'C', parent: 'B' } }, 'B', 'C')).toBe(true)

tests.description: D is not an ancestor of C (diverged)
tests.expr: expect(isAncestor({ A: { id: 'A', parent: null }, B: { id: 'B', parent: 'A' }, C: { id: 'C', parent: 'B' }, D: { id: 'D', parent: 'B' } }, 'D', 'C')).toBe(false)

tests.description: a commit is its own ancestor

items.explanation: Walking backward from the descendant through parent pointers and checking for the ancestor at each step is exactly how git determines whether a fast-forward is possible — no divergence means the walk reaches the ancestor before running out of parents.

items.prompt: Implement `rebase(commits, localCommitIds, newBaseId)`, matching this unit's L3: replay each commit in `localCommitIds` (in order) onto `newBaseId`, returning an array of new commit objects, each with an id of the original id plus `'`, chained parent-to-parent.

tests.expr: expect(rebase({ D: { id: 'D', parent: 'B', message: 'fix' } }, ['D'], 'C')).toEqual([{ id: "D'", parent: 'C', message: 'fix' }])

expect(rebase({ D: { id: 'D', parent: 'B', message: 'fix' }, E: { id: 'E', parent: 'D', message: 'tweak' } }, ['D', 'E'], 'C')).toEqual([{ id: "D'", parent: 'C', message: 'fix' }, { id: "E'", parent: "D'", message: 'tweak' }])

items.explanation: Each commit is replayed with a new id and the previous replayed commit as its parent — this is exactly the 'one at a time, each on top of the last' process a real rebase performs, made explicit as a loop.

items.prompt: What did L3's `canFastForward` check actually return for Monday's scenario (local at B, remote at C, no local commits)?
choices: true — local's HEAD (B) is a direct ancestor of remote's HEAD (C)
false — Monday's pull also required a merge commit
It threw an error, since B and C are different commits
true, but only because remote had zero commits ahead of local
items.explanation: With no local commits since the last sync, B is directly in C's ancestry, so `canFastForward` returns true — exactly matching Monday's clean pull.
items.reference:
Monday vs. Tuesday, measured
Monday: canFastForward(B, C) → true
Tuesday: canFastForward(D, C) → false

Why: One local commit is exactly what turned Monday's clean pull into Tuesday's merge commit — nothing about size or content mattered.

items.prompt: What did L3's `canFastForward` check actually return for Tuesday's scenario (local at D, remote at C, both descended from B)?
choices: false — local's HEAD (D) is not an ancestor of remote's HEAD (C), since they diverged at B
true — Tuesday's pull was also a clean fast-forward
It returned an error because D doesn't exist in the commit graph
true, because both D and C eventually trace back to A
items.explanation: D and C are siblings, both children of B — walking backward from C never reaches D, so `canFastForward` correctly returns false, matching Tuesday's merge commit.
items.reference:
Monday vs. Tuesday, measured
Monday: canFastForward(B, C) → true
Tuesday: canFastForward(D, C) → false

Why: One local commit is exactly what turned Monday's clean pull into Tuesday's merge commit — nothing about size or content mattered.

items.prompt: According to L3's failure-modes table, does rebase avoid conflicts entirely by not creating a merge commit?
choices: No — rebase still reconciles content and can still hit conflicts while replaying each commit, it just records the result differently
Yes, rebase is specifically designed to be conflict-free
Yes, because rebase only works on commits with no code changes
No, rebase always produces more conflicts than a merge would
items.explanation: Not creating a merge commit is a difference in how the result is recorded, not a difference in whether the underlying content actually needs reconciling — replaying a commit can still conflict with the new base.
items.reference:
No merge commit ≠ no reconciliation
rebase still reconciles content per commit
can still hit conflicts while replaying

Why: The absence of a merge commit is a recording choice, not evidence that reconciliation never happened.

items.prompt: Why is it a mistake to assume 'no merge commit' means 'nothing was reconciled' when a rebase completes?
choices: Rebase reconciles each replayed commit's content against the new base individually — it just doesn't record that reconciliation as a single visible merge commit
Rebase literally cannot change any file content, ever
Because rebase always fails loudly if any reconciliation would be needed
Because git deletes all evidence of reconciliation after a rebase completes
items.explanation: The reconciliation work still happens per commit during replay — rebase just chooses not to leave a merge commit as the visible trace of it.
items.reference:
No merge commit ≠ no reconciliation
rebase still reconciles content per commit
can still hit conflicts while replaying

Why: The absence of a merge commit is a recording choice, not evidence that reconciliation never happened.
